stem: A patient with a family history of malignant hyperthermia is undergoing elective surgery. What can you do to prevent it?

opts.t: Avoid depolarizing muscle relaxants and volatile agents
Avoid volatile and just use depolarizing muscle relaxants
Use depolarizing but make sure dantrolene is available in OR

expl: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine (a depolarizing relaxant). Prevention = avoid both (use TIVA); dantrolene is the treatment.

why.C: Dantrolene availability does not make a trigger safe; you still avoid it.
why.D: No need to postpone — just use a trigger-free anesthetic.

stem: An obese patient just finished day surgery in the morning for right inguinal hernia repair. In the recovery room the patient has a fever and is in severe pain. The wound and surrounding area all the way down to the thigh is red, tender with areas of discolouration and crepitus. What do you do?

opts.t: Broad spectrum Antibiotic and immediate surgical debridement
Broad spectrum antibiotic and consult ID

expl: Severe pain, redness spreading to the thigh, discoloration and crepitus within hours of surgery = necrotizing infection → antibiotics + immediate debridement.

stem: 24 yo female who underwent excision of lipoma on the left lateral thigh. Now she presented with severe pain in her left thigh enabling her from ambulation, her pain associated with high fever, erythema, swelling and crepitus. It's also associated with bullae and bruising. She noticed that the colour of her thigh is rapidly changing to darker. Which of the following is the next step?

opts.t: Admission to icu with septic screening
Broad spectrum ABx with urgent surgical debridement.

expl: Severe pain, fever, bullae, bruising, crepitus and rapidly darkening skin after minor surgery = necrotizing fasciitis. Treatment is a surgical emergency: broad-spectrum antibiotics plus urgent debridement.

why.A: Antibiotics alone don't penetrate necrotic tissue; mortality rises with delay.
why.B: This is not an allergic reaction.
why.C: ICU care may be needed, but surgery must not be delayed.

stem: A female patient had surgery 2 days ago. She had severe pain that limited ambulation. Now she has a fever of 40.2 C. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Fever on post-op day 2 with pain limiting deep breathing/ambulation is classically atelectasis (UTI, SSI and pneumonia come later).

stem: A smoker, otherwise healthy man is undergoing an elective surgery, which of the following would be best to prevent postop pulmonary complications?

opts.t: Routine preoperative pulmonary function testing for all smokers

expl: Stopping smoking 4–6 weeks before surgery lets ciliary function and sputum clear, lowering post-op pulmonary complications (the doctor gave ~6 weeks).

why.A: Correct — the only option that removes the cause in time.
why.B: Treats bronchospasm after the fact; doesn't prevent complications.
why.C: Spirometry exercises help, but stopping smoking has the biggest effect.
why.D: Routine PFTs for all smokers are not indicated and don't prevent anything.

stem: A 55-year-old man is post-operative day 1 following elective abdominal surgery. He is a heavy smoker and is becoming agitated, restless, and irritable, repeatedly asking to leave the ward to smoke. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Sedate the patient with intravenous benzodiazepines
Attempt to convince the patient to tolerate symptoms without treatment
Allow the patient to smoke under supervision

expl: Agitation, restlessness and craving on POD 1 in a heavy smoker = nicotine withdrawal → nicotine replacement patch.

why.A: Benzodiazepines don't treat withdrawal and cause respiratory depression post-op.
why.C: Untreated withdrawal causes distress and poor cooperation.
why.D: Smoking impairs wound healing and oxygenation.

stem: 35-year-old man develops sudden hypercarbia, tachycardia, muscle rigidity, and rising temperature shortly after surgery. He is postoperative and was exposed to volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

opts.t: Administer IV dantrolene, provide supportive care
Give IV corticosteroids to reduce inflammation

expl: Hypercarbia, rigidity, tachycardia and rising temperature after volatiles + succinylcholine = malignant hyperthermia → stop triggers, give IV dantrolene, cool and support.

stem: A 65-year-old patient is on postoperative day 3 receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics. He develops mild abdominal pain and watery diarrhea. Vital signs are stable, and there are no signs of severe infection. Stool tests confirm Clostridium difficile infection (CDI). What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Give oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin

expl: Non-severe C. difficile infection is treated with oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin (and stopping the offending antibiotic when possible).

why.A: Helpful but not sufficient treatment alone.
why.B: IV vancomycin doesn't reach the colon.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents 5 days after abdominal surgery. On examination, the surgical site shows a soft, fluctuant swelling without erythema, pus, or bleeding. The patient has no fever or systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A soft fluctuant swelling without erythema, pus, fever or bleeding = seroma (serous fluid collection).

why.C: Would show erythema, pus or fever.

stem: A 45-year-old woman 2 hours after thyroidectomy develops progressive neck swelling, difficulty breathing, and stridor. Examination shows a rapidly expanding neck hematoma. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

opts.t: Secure the airway first with endotrachial intubation , then evacuate the hematoma
Incise and evacuate the hematoma immediately at bedside without airway management
Obtain a CT scan of the neck

expl: Source key B: an expanding post-thyroidectomy hematoma compresses the airway — open the wound and evacuate the clot at the bedside immediately; this relieves the obstruction and often makes intubation unnecessary or easier.

why.A: Intubation can be impossible through a compressed, edematous airway — decompress first.

stem: A 56-year-old man is in the ICU after major abdominal trauma and massive fluid resuscitation. He is hemodynamically stable but develops progressive abdominal distension, decreased urine output, and increasing ventilatory pressures. Measurement of intra-abdominal pressure shows a value of 32 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction (oliguria, rising airway pressures) = abdominal compartment syndrome (32 mmHg here, after massive resuscitation).

why.B: Possible cause, but the diagnosis is ACS.

stem: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery. His baseline oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Which of the following is the most effective strategy to prevent postoperative respiratory failure?

opts.t: Effective pain management and incentive spirometry

expl: In severe COPD, post-op respiratory failure comes from shallow breathing because of pain and atelectasis. Good analgesia + incentive spirometry keeps the lungs expanded.

why.A: Pre-op rehab helps but is not the most effective single measure in this setting.
why.C: Oxygen alone doesn't prevent atelectasis or sputum retention.
why.D: Chest physiotherapy alone, without pain control, is less effective.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is on postoperative day 1 after total thyroidectomy. She develops tingling around her mouth and fingers, and Chvostek’s sign is positive. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
expl: Symptomatic hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy (perioral tingling, Chvostek) → IV calcium gluconate.

why.C: Check Mg if refractory, but calcium comes first.

stem: A 60-year-old patient is postoperative on day 2. He has tachycardia (HR 110), tachypnea (RR 25), temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, and WBC 13,000. Which of the following is the most appropriate classification?
expl: SIRS = ≥2 of: T >38/<36, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12k/<4k. He has all four, normal BP and no organ dysfunction.

why.A: These numbers exceed the normal post-op response.

stem: A 50-year-old patient is postoperative day 5 after abdominal surgery. He develops purulent discharge from the surgical site but is hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and has no systemic symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Return to the operating room for debridement
Open and clean the wound at the bedside, change dressings regularly

expl: A superficial SSI with pus in a stable, afebrile patient → open the wound, clean, and dress regularly (drainage is the treatment).

why.A: OR debridement is for deep/necrotizing infection.
why.B: IV antibiotics are not needed without systemic signs.

stem: A 65-year-old patient is postoperative day 2 after abdominal surgery. He develops tachycardia, hypotension, fever, and cold extremities, with elevated lactate, Bedside point-of-care ultrasound shows a collapsed inferior vena cava (IVC) and a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology of his condition?

opts.t: Systemic vasodilation with decreased systemic vascular resistance (SVR)

expl: Fever + hypotension with a hyperdynamic LV and collapsed IVC = distributive (septic) shock from systemic vasodilation and low SVR.

why.A: Pump failure would give a poor LV and full IVC.
why.B: Hypovolemia gives a collapsed IVC too, but fever and a hyperdynamic heart point to sepsis.

stem: A 58-year-old man develops an enterocutaneous fistula 2 days after surgery for bowel obstruction. The fistula output is <100 mL/day, and the remaining bowel appears normal. He has no fever. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Continue enteral feeding and provide wound care

expl: A low-output (<200 mL/day, here <100) fistula with normal distal bowel, no sepsis or obstruction usually closes spontaneously → continue enteral nutrition, protect the skin, monitor fluids.

why.B: TPN is for high-output fistulas or when enteral feeding fails.
why.C: Surgery is for fistulas that fail to close (usually after 6–12 weeks).

stem: A 56-year-old female with suspected choledocholithiasis undergoes ERCP, which reveals biliary stones without bile duct wall thickening. Six hours after the procedure, she develops severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting. Laboratory analysis shows serum lipase elevated to more than three times the upper limit of normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

opts.t: Acute pancreatitis related to ERCP procedure

expl: Epigastric pain to the back with lipase >3× normal hours after ERCP = post-ERCP pancreatitis, the commonest ERCP complication.

stem: A patient develops fever 48 hours after surgery. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Classic teaching: fever within 48 h after surgery is most often atelectasis (the "5 Ws": wind, water, wound, walking, wonder drugs).

stem: A patient with massive intra-abdominal bleeding underwent exploratory laparotomy and was given 6 units of packed red blood cells. Then she was found to have blood oozing from the central and peripheral lines with low platelets (33), prolonged PT,PTT,INR what do you give next?
expl: After massive transfusion, oozing from lines with prolonged PT/PTT = dilutional coagulopathy → replace clotting factors with FFP (and platelets, which are 33).

why.C: An adjunct for fibrinolysis, not the main deficit.

stem: A smoker is scheduled for elective surgery. When should they stop smoking to minimize postoperative complications?
expl: 4–6 weeks of cessation reduces post-op pulmonary complications.

stem: A patient presents on day 3 post-operation with fever, local abdominal tenderness, erythema, and purulent discharge from the wound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, local tenderness, erythema and purulent wound discharge on day 3 = surgical site infection.

why.C: Dehiscence = wound separation with serosanguinous fluid.

stem: 19 y/o present to the ER with perforated appendicitis and we did laparoscopic appendectomy with multiple time wash the abdomen we discharge the patient and he present later with persistent fever with RLQ tenderness without sign of peritonitis HR and blood pressure is normal WBC is 14 after doing CT we found 6 CM RLQ collection what is the best management?
expl: A stable patient with a 6 cm well-defined abscess → antibiotics + image-guided percutaneous drainage (less invasive than surgery).

why.A: Surgery is for failed percutaneous drainage or peritonitis.
why.D: Antibiotics alone don't drain a large collection.

stem: 45 years old female taking anticoagulation because she had a valve replacement surgery a long time ago (forgot which surgery but it was laparotomy I think ) so they stopped her coagulation before surgery. 2 days after the surgery her anticoagulation was started again the nurse noticed the site of the wound was swollen and had skin color changes. When you examined it after pressing on the wound you noticed blood clots oozing from the wound site. What could be the cause?
expl: The source option "hamartoma" is a typo for HEMATOMA: swelling, skin discoloration and clots oozing from the wound after anticoagulation was restarted = wound hematoma.

why.B: Abscess would show pus, fever, erythema.
why.C: Seroma is clear fluid without discoloration; dehiscence shows separation/serosanguinous fluid.

stem: A 50 year old man did surgery a couple of days ago, currently in the ICU unable to wean from the ventilator, although he was successfully extubated after surgery. You suspect the patient has SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) which of the following supports your diagnosis?
expl: Temperature >38 and WBC >12,000 are two SIRS criteria.

stem: A 50 years old man did surgery a couple of days ago, currently in the ICU unable to wean from the ventilator, although he was successfully extubated after surgery. You suspect the patient has SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) which of the following supports your diagnosis?
expl: Source key: gastroduodenal (stress) ulcer — a recognized consequence of the systemic stress response/SIRS in ICU patients. The question is poorly recalled.

why.A: An NG tube doesn't support SIRS.
why.D: Renal injury would suggest organ dysfunction (sepsis), not SIRS.

stem: The patient did thyroidectomy and after that she has muscle cramps and abdominal pain with deep tendon reflex, what is the cause?
expl: After thyroidectomy, parathyroid injury → hypocalcemia → cramps, tetany, hyperreflexia, abdominal cramps.

why.D: Hypocalcemia raises phosphate, but symptoms are from calcium.

stem: Patient done splenectomy he developed fever and rash post op
expl: Fever (± rash/purpura) after splenectomy = overwhelming post-splenectomy infection until proven otherwise (encapsulated organisms). The source writes "correct answer is OPSI".

why.B: Pancreatic tail injury can cause pancreatitis/fistula but doesn't explain fever with rash.

stem: patient just had thyroidectomy and now presented with a strider and difficulty breathing. The doctor noticed the swelling in the incision area. What is the most likely cause? expecting hematoma Recall supplied without a complete set of labelled choices.
expl: Swelling at the incision with stridor and respiratory distress soon after thyroidectomy = expanding hematoma compressing the airway.
ansText: Neck hematoma (the source expected "hematoma") — stridor + swelling at the incision after thyroidectomy → open the wound at the bedside and evacuate the clot.

stem: patient post duodenal ulcer surgery Billroth 2 he developed fever and tachycardia what is the most likely cause? Duodenal stump leak Recall supplied without a complete set of labelled choices.
expl: After Billroth II, the closed duodenal stump can blow out (usually days 3–7) → fever, tachycardia, peritonitis/sepsis.

stem: A patient with perioral numbness, tingling, and possibly tetany after a thyroidectomy ,What is the abnormality expected in her labs?

opts.t: Low Ca, low phos, low PTH
Low Ca, low phos, high PTH
High Ca, low phos, low PTH
High Ca, high phos, high PTH

expl: Source key A. After thyroidectomy, parathyroid injury → low PTH and low calcium. In true hypoparathyroidism phosphate RISES (less renal phosphate excretion); low phosphate with low calcium fits "hungry bone" syndrome. Option A is the only choice with low Ca + low PTH.

why.B: High PTH = secondary hyperparathyroidism (e.g. vitamin D deficiency).
why.D: Primary hyperparathyroidism pattern (phosphate would be low).

stem: A 55 y/o man who is receiving total parenteral nutrition through the right subclavian PICC for short bowel syndrome developed high temperature (39C). Two blood cultures were positive for staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?

opts.t: Remove the PICC, send tip for culture and administer antibiotics
Change the PICC over the wire

expl: S. aureus bacteremia from a central line (PICC) → remove the line (send the tip for culture) and give a long antibiotic course. S. aureus is never a contaminant.

why.B: Exchanging over a wire keeps an infected tract.
why.C: Lock therapy isn't enough for S. aureus.

stem: A 68 y/o woman was admitted through the ER with an abscess in the right foot. She underwent surgical drainage of the abscess with an intravenous therapeutic course of Cefuxime. Five days later. She developed diarrhea with mucus. Which of the following organisms is the most likely underlying cause of the diarrhea?
srcNote: Source note (431 A Q53): pseudomembranous colitis
expl: Diarrhea after a course of a cephalosporin = C. difficile (pseudomembranous colitis).

stem: After oesophagectomy, the surgical drain puts out ~700 mL of serous fluid, which increases and turns white after oral intake. What is the likely cause?
srcNote: Source note (436 A Q16): Answer: B, answer is confirmed when Q was reviewed with the course organiser
expl: After oesophagectomy, drainage that turns milky white once oral (fat) intake starts = chyle leak from thoracic duct injury (chylothorax). Confirmed by the course organiser.
ansText: Thoracic duct injury → chylothorax. Milky fluid appears once fat is eaten (chylomicrons; triglycerides > 110 mg/dL). Treat: NPO/TPN or medium-chain-triglyceride diet ± octreotide; re-operate to ligate the duct if output stays high.

stem: patient Underwent Multiple laparotomy. Then become with enterocutaneous fistula What electrolytes imbalance is expected:-
expl: Enterocutaneous (small-bowel) fistula loses bicarbonate-rich fluid → metabolic acidosis.

stem: A patient is 1-day post-op of a left lower lobe lung procedure, he was not in pain and he had no fever, his urine output was adequate. His vitals were 160 bpm BP 90/60. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: New AF is the commonest arrhythmia after lung resection (atrial irritation/inflammation); HR 160 in a well patient without pain or fever.

why.D: 160 without pain/fever/bleeding is unlikely to be sinus.

stem: After surgery, you notice your patient having abdominal bloating and abdominal distension, the x-ray shows an air-fluid level. What are you going to do next?

opts.t: keep patient Npo, and nasogastric decompression
Do CT to confirm the diagnosis

expl: Post-op distension with air-fluid levels (ileus or early obstruction) → conservative: NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, correct electrolytes.

why.C: CT only if not settling or signs of strangulation.

stem: Pt underwent total parathyroidectomy. 1 day post op he developed numbness and tingling sensation circumorally. Which of the following is the most likely electrolyte abnormality?
expl: Total parathyroidectomy → hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcemia (perioral numbness/tingling).

stem: A patient who underwent surgery and during rounds the physician noticed serosanguinous discharge and upon pressure on the gauze the wound produced more serosanguinous discharge and the sutures were intact with a bulge. No pus or erythema was noticed. What is the cause?
expl: Serosanguinous ("salmon-coloured") discharge that increases with pressure, intact skin sutures and a bulge = fascial (partial) dehiscence — the classic warning sign.

why.D: Hematoma gives blood/clots, not serosanguinous fluid.

stem: Diabetic patient removed lipoma suture with pain and erythema at site but otherwise normal how to deal with this patient
expl: Source key: proper hand hygiene — the most effective infection-prevention measure. Mild erythema without systemic illness doesn't need antibiotics.

why.A: Not needed for mild local signs.
why.D: Reasonable care, but hand hygiene is keyed.

stem: Patient in ICU bleeds from NGT, he was intubated >48 hrs and on vasopressors. Ordered for him EGD (esophagogastroduodenoscopy). What should be done to prevent this complication?
expl: Ventilation >48 h and coagulopathy/shock are indications for stress-ulcer prophylaxis with acid suppression (PPI/H2 blocker).

why.B: Enteral feeding actually protects the mucosa.
why.D: Used for variceal prophylaxis, not stress ulcers.

stem: A 42 y/o woman presented with a low grade fever for the past 3 days. On examination, you found a unilateral swollen leg that became painful when you stretched her calf. Which of the following is the best management ?
expl: Unilateral swollen leg with calf pain on stretch (Homan's) → suspect DVT → confirm with duplex ultrasound before anticoagulation.

why.B: Confirm first (unless very high suspicion with delay).

stem: A case about a patient who has done a successful non-complicated laparoscopic appendectomy, and asked about how to prevent surgical infections in this patient ?

opts.t: Pre-op cefazolin, during the surgery, and for 72 hours post-op

expl: For uncomplicated appendicitis/appendectomy, a peri-operative dose of a cephalosporin + metronidazole (covers gut aerobes and anaerobes) is enough; no prolonged post-op course.

why.A: Cefazolin lacks anaerobic cover and 72 hours post-op is unnecessary.

stem: A case of a chron’s patient who underwent hemicolectomy as a management for his symptoms. However, he presented a few days later post-op complaining of signs and symptoms of local peritonitis. What’s the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms ?
expl: Local peritonitis a few days after a bowel resection with anastomosis → anastomotic leak until proven otherwise.

why.B: Causes recurrence later, not acute peritonitis.

stem: A 32 year old man presented with ruptured appendicitis. A Laparoscopic procedure was done. 4 days post-op, he had a fever and and a right lower quadrant pain, but the wound looked OK with no redness or discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever and RLQ pain on day 4 after appendectomy for a ruptured appendix with a normal wound = intra-abdominal (pelvic/RLQ) abscess — an organ-space SSI.

why.A: Cecal perforation/leak would give peritonitis and sepsis.

stem: A patient post laparotomy presents after 6 days with pain and erythema at site no fever no discharge and otherwise what is the best way to manage this patient?
expl: Pain and erythema without fever or discharge = superficial wound problem → local care (daily cleansing).

stem: A patient post gastric sleeve developed signs of septic shock. Which one of the following is the reason?
expl: Septic shock after sleeve gastrectomy = staple-line leak until proven otherwise (most at the angle of His).

why.A: Doesn't cause septic shock at this stage typically.
why.C: Correct (the source says "stable leak"; a leak causing septic shock).

stem: A pt who had median sternotomy and developed a keloid scar, and asks about what to tell the pt to expect to have ?
expl: Source key A (one version also marked D). Keloids are typically itchy and can be painful; they keep growing beyond the scar rather than fluctuating.

why.C: Can occur but itching is the classic symptom.
why.D: The alternative mark in the source.

stem: 51 y/o man who underwent abdomino-perineal resection for low rectal cancer 5 days ago. Was complaining of chest pain and dyspnea. Physical examination was normal. CBC and cardiac enzymes were normal. Temperature 37.2, Blood pressure 85\50 mmHg, Pulse 120 beat\min. Which of the following is the common appropriate diagnosis investigation?
srcNote: (Miscellaneous) Source note (433 A Q44): increased risk of PE post OP Source note (432 F Q59): Pulmonary Embolism � spiral CT
expl: Post-op pelvic surgery, chest pain, dyspnea, hypotension with normal enzymes → PE → CT pulmonary angiography.

stem: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) is associated with which one of these complications?
srcNote: (Nutrition in surgical patients) Source note (429 F Q14): other complications: dehydration and electrolyte Imbalances, thrombosis.
expl: TPN's concentrated dextrose commonly causes hyperglycemia (also line sepsis, thrombosis, electrolyte and liver problems).

stem: 38 y o women who underwent exploratory laparotomy. Found to have multiple subcutaneous hematoma with bleeding from the site of intravenous cannula insertion. Lab values showed prolonged PT, PTT and INR with low platelet and high platelet degradation products. Which of the following can help for diagnosing this condition?
srcNote: (Miscellaneous) Source note (433 A Q45): “disseminated intravascular coagulation. “ ( surgical complication ) Source note (432 F Q60): DIC Source note (429 F Q9): diagnostic for DIC Source figure: 432 F Q60
expl: Bleeding from cannula sites, prolonged PT/PTT, low platelets and high fibrin degradation products = DIC; D-dimer is the key diagnostic test.

stem: A 28 year old man, 4 days post-exploratory laparotomy for perforated acute appendicitis with grossly distended abdomen and mild generalized discomfort, sluggish bowel sounds, vomiting and constipation. Investigations revealed white blood counts: 15 * 109 (normal range 3.5-10.5 *109) and multiple air fluid levels in the abdominal X-ray.Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Distension, sluggish bowel sounds and air-fluid levels 4 days after laparotomy for perforated appendicitis = paralytic ileus (WBC can still be raised after peritonitis).

stem: 65 year old male post open cholecystectomy, can’t tolerate food on continuous NGT suction, which of the following abnormalities is expected to be in this pt?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: Continuous NG suction removes gastric HCl → metabolic alkalosis (with hypokalemia and hypochloremia).

stem: A 65 y/o man who is receiving total parenteral nutrition for high output small bowel fistula with persistent hyperglycemia inspite of insulin infusion. Which of the following is the appropriate step in management?
expl: New, persistent hyperglycemia on TPN despite insulin often signals hidden sepsis — look for the source.

why.A: Oral agents are irrelevant on TPN.

stem: Patient presented with sepsis, had a subclavian central line inserted. 2 hours later, he became tachycardic, his BP and O2 saturation dropped, what’s the most likely cause? (incomplete question)
srcNote: (Practical Procedures and Investigation of Surgical Patients)
expl: Hypotension, tachycardia and desaturation shortly after a subclavian line → iatrogenic tension pneumothorax.

stem: Which of the following nerves can be injured during surgery for inguinal hernia repair?

opts.t: Ilioinguinal nerve, iliohypogastric nerve, genitofemoral nerve
Pudendal nerve, iliohypogastric nerve, popliteal nerve
Ilioinguinal nerve, pudendal nerve, iliohypogastric nerve
Ilioinguinal nerve, femoral nerve, genitofemoral nerve

expl: Inguinal hernia repair can injure the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and genitofemoral nerves (chronic groin pain/numbness).

why.B: Pudendal and popliteal aren't in the field.

stem: A 45-year-old women on TPN for high output small bowel fistula. The TPN has been abruptly stopped, and the patient transferred for abdominal ultrasound. When the patient arrived to the radiology department, she was anxious, irritable, confused and she developed seizure and loss of consciousness. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: TPN contains concentrated glucose with high endogenous insulin; abrupt stop → rebound hypoglycemia (anxiety, confusion, seizures, coma).

stem: A 60-year old man, who is known diabetic and hypertensive admitted as a routine case for laparoscopic transabdominal right inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia. After surgery the patient was transferred to the recovery room. Which of the following specifically need to be monitored?
srcNote: (Principles of laparoscopic surgery) (Surgical Complications) (THIS Q confused many students Bc in the previous years the Answer was B, but then we figured out based on our Marks that the right answer is A)
expl: A diabetic hypertensive patient after GA is at risk of a (silent) perioperative MI → specifically monitor for MI. Students confirmed by their marks that the key is A (earlier years thought B).

why.B: Earlier assumed answer; airway is monitored for everyone.

stem: a patient presented after a trauma with splenic rupture. He had a splenectomy. A year later he presented with hypotension, fever, and septic shock. What is the most likely organism?
expl: After splenectomy, overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is caused by encapsulated organisms — mostly Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: 45 y/o woman had a history of open appendectomy 2 years ago, came to the ER complaining of abdominal pain and distension, there was an X-ray pic, (incomplete) What is the management? Source figure: 434 Q56
srcNote: (Principles of Laparoscopic Surgery) there’s adhesions we can’t go laparoscopically Source note (434 Q56): (Intestinal obstruction)
expl: Source key: exploratory laparotomy — adhesions from previous surgery make laparoscopy difficult. (Today most adhesive SBO is managed conservatively first unless strangulation/failure; follow the key.)

stem: A 65-year-old gentleman is admitted to the ICU with sepsis following perforated diverticulitis. In the ICU a triple lumen central venous catheter is inserted into the right internal jugular vein. 2 hours later, the patient is increasingly restless. He is tachypnic with RR of 30/min. His O2 requirements have increased and his O2 saturation is dropping. His vasopressor requirements have increased as his BP is dropping. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Chest trauma) Source note (437 A Q8): Ans. D (Q was repeated and one of them was canceled) (Chest trauma)
expl: Restlessness, tachypnoea, rising O₂ and vasopressor needs shortly after an IJ line = iatrogenic (tension) pneumothorax — check breath sounds and decompress.

why.A: Possible but rarer; sudden collapse during insertion.
why.B: Not linked to line insertion 2 h earlier.
why.C: Already present; doesn't explain acute worsening.

stem: Which one of the following is the most common complication of endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)?
expl: The commonest complication of ERCP is pancreatitis (3–5%); others are bleeding (sphincterotomy), cholangitis and perforation.

stem: A 35-year-old woman had undergone thyroidectomy for a suspicious thyroid mass. Several hours postoperatively she developed progressive swelling under the incision. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
expl: Progressive swelling under a thyroidectomy wound hours post-op = hematoma → wound exploration/evacuation before it obstructs the airway.

why.B: Laryngoscopy assesses nerve palsy, not a hematoma.

stem: Which of the following is true regarding why obese pt are at an increased risk of complications during surgery

opts.t: Procedures could take a longer time

expl: Obese patients are at higher risk partly because procedures take longer (and are technically harder), plus airway, wound and VTE problems.

stem: Which of the following is correct regarding Thyroid surgeries

opts.t: There’s a possibility of developing Myxedema coma post surgery in Hypothyroid pt

expl: Hypothyroid patients may develop myxedema coma after surgery — another reason to make them euthyroid before elective surgery.

stem: A young female pt underwent simple external hemorrhoidectomy under epidural anesthesia, complaining of headache 24 hrs post-op. Which of the following is not part of the initial management?
srcNote: (Practical Procedures and Investigation of Surgical Patients)
expl: Post-dural-puncture headache: initial management = bed rest, fluids, analgesics (caffeine). Epidural blood patch is NOT initial; it's for persistent headache.

stem: Tight control of sugar level in a diabetic patient undergoing surgery:

opts.t: Decrease the incidence of deep wound infection

expl: Tight peri-operative glucose control lowers surgical-site (deep wound) infection.

why.B: Not a benefit of glucose control.
why.C: Phagocytosis improves, but the tested outcome is fewer infections.
why.D: Wrong — glucose control clearly improves outcomes.

stem: A 47 y/o gentleman is in the operating room for emergent perforated duodenal ulcer. Prior to the OR patient was complaining of abdominal pain and was hemodynamically unstable. What can be done in the postoperative period to decrease morbidity and complications of the surgery?
expl: An unstable patient after emergency surgery for perforation benefits from ICU monitoring/support post-op.

stem: Local complication of angiogram and angioplasty?
srcNote: (local: pseudoanyeurysm, systemic: contrast induced nephropathy & anaphylaxis)
expl: Local access-site complications of angiography: hematoma, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, dissection, thrombosis. Systemic ones: contrast nephropathy and anaphylaxis.

stem: What’s the immediate common complication post total thyroidectomy?
expl: Transient hypocalcaemia from parathyroid injury/devascularisation is the commonest early complication after total thyroidectomy.

why.D: Expected after total thyroidectomy (replaced), not a "complication".

stem: scenario about a patient 5 days post op developed SOB and chest pain, fever ….. chest xray shows consolidation on right lung(?). Pulmonary vessels are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, dyspnoea and chest pain on POD 5 with consolidation and normal pulmonary vessels → hospital-acquired pneumonia (>48 h after admission).

why.A: CXR is usually normal; vessels would be abnormal on CTPA.

stem: A 45-year-old woman was admitted through ER with cholecystitis. She underwent cholecystectomy with an intravenous therapeutic course of ceftriaxone. Seven days later. She developed diarrhoea mixed with mild fresh blood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Diarrhoea with blood after a course of ceftriaxone = C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis.

stem: A 20 year old African American woman presented to the clinic complaining of swelling in the earlobe after 2 months of ear piercing. What’s the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: ( skin , soft tissue and wound management)
expl: A swelling of the earlobe months after piercing in a dark-skinned person = keloid.

stem: A 41-year-old man underwent blood transfusion for postoperative bleeding. He developed pain at the site of the infusion with fever and chest tightness after a few minutes of the transfusion. Which of the following is the most likely blood transfusion complication?
srcNote: (Miscellaneous) Source note (436 A Q26): - Hemolytic reaction present with chest and flank pain (Miscellaneous) Source figure: 432 F Q26
expl: Fever, chest tightness and pain at the infusion site within minutes = acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO incompatibility) → stop transfusion.

why.B: Possible, but site pain + chest/flank pain is classic hemolysis.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is recovering from a thyroidectomy. The patient starts to complain of tingling and numbness in the face, toes, and fingers What is your FIRST action?
expl: Source key B — confirm hypocalcaemia with a calcium level first (and give calcium promptly). With severe symptoms (tetany, laryngospasm, seizures) IV calcium gluconate is given immediately.

why.A: Magnesium is checked if calcium doesn't correct.

stem: A 48-year-old male had inguinal hernia repair, following his surgery he failed to urinate on his own, following two in and out bladder catheterization he still couldn't urinate. What is the management for this patient’s urinary retention?

opts.t: Discharge home and follow up with urology next week
Observation as this should resolve spontaneously
Insert foley catheter with trial of void in few days

expl: Persistent post-op retention after two in-out catheterizations → indwelling Foley and a trial without catheter in a few days.

stem: A 45-year-old man, who has hypertension and controlled type 2 diabetes, presented 4 days post-exploratory laparotomy for perforated acute appendicitis with grossly distended abdomen and mild generalized discomfort. He has sluggish bowel sounds, vomiting and constipation. His vitals are normal, and his investigations revealed white blood count of 8 (normal range 3.5-10.5) and multiple air-fluid levels in the abdominal X-ray. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Post-laparotomy (peritonitis) distension, vomiting, sluggish bowel sounds, air-fluid levels with normal WBC and vitals on day 4 → paralytic ileus.

why.C: Obstruction gives hyperactive (not sluggish) sounds; early adhesive SBO is less likely.

stem: Scenario about diabetic patient who undergo resection of lipoma came after with mild pain in the surgical area , examination show erythematous edge and pain , (removal of suture showed no pus (similar) the remaining of question was excluding abscess) what is the diagnosis?
expl: Erythema and mild pain without pus after a lipoma excision = superficial skin infection (cellulitis of the wound edge).

why.C: Suture allergy isn't the classic answer.

stem: A 48-year-old female was admitted through the emergency department with abdominal pain, abdominal distention, nausea and vomiting for three days. She hasn’t passed gas or stool for 1 day. Her past medical history includes hypertension, dyslipidemia and open appendectomy Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
expl: Obstruction after a previous open appendectomy → adhesions/bands are the commonest cause of SBO.

why.C: Possible but less likely with this history.

stem: A 32-year old man underwent open appendectomy for a perforated acute appendicitis. He was started on therapeutic course of intravenous cefuroxime and metronidazole. Five days later the wound became painful, swollen, and red with pus discharge between the sutures Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?

opts.t: Open the wound and daily dressing

expl: Surgical-site infection with pus between the sutures → open the wound (remove sutures), drain and dress.

why.C: Not needed when pus is obvious.

stem: A 51-year-old man who underwent abdomino-perineal resection for low rectal cancer 5 days ago, was complaining of chest pain and dyspnea. Physical examination was normal. CBC and cardiac enzymes were normal. Temp: 37.2, BP:85/50 mmHg, pulse: 120 beat/min. Which of the following is the most common appropriate diagnostic investigation?
expl: Post-op pelvic surgery, chest pain, dyspnoea, hypotension and tachycardia with normal enzymes → PE → CT pulmonary angiography.

stem: An otherwise healthy patient with good nutritional status underwent gynecomastia excision Which of the following wound healing effects would be seen after prescribing multivitamins to the patient?
expl: Vitamin supplements improve healing only if the patient is deficient. In a well-nourished patient they have no effect.

stem: Which of the following is not a complication of suprapubic catheter insertion?
expl: Suprapubic catheter risks: infection, bleeding/pelvic vessel injury, bowel perforation — the liver is far away.

stem: A smoker patient undergoing lung surgery. When should he stop smoking before the surgery to reduce the risk for post-operative lung problems?
expl: Stop smoking at least ~6 weeks before lung surgery (the doctor's example was ~6 weeks).

why.B: Longer than needed for the standard answer.
why.D: 4 weeks is the minimum; for lung surgery the keyed answer is 6 weeks.

stem: A patient with lipoma in the back 3-4 cm came and you took the lipoma out, a month later he came in with pain at the site of injury and erythema around the wound with no discharge or abscess. What is the management?
expl: Pain and erythema a month after surgery without discharge or abscess → superficial problem → local wound care.

stem: A patient needed 2 liters of blood and it was given in central line what is the most common complication?
expl: Source key: tension pneumothorax — the most dangerous immediate complication of central venous access (pneumothorax is the classic insertion complication). Infection is commoner later.

stem: Which of the following is the Least common complication for central line insertion ?
expl: Myocarditis isn't a central-line complication; hemothorax, air embolism and infection are.

stem: Patient is presented with abdominal pain and mild distension , abdominal examination shows multiple scars from previous surgeries , rectal exam show empty rectal vault

opts.t: CT abdomen with oral and IV contrast

expl: Suspected adhesive obstruction (multiple scars, empty rectum, distension) → CT abdomen with oral and IV contrast to confirm, find the transition point and look for strangulation.

stem: A 29- year old man presented to the Emergency department with acute appendicitis. He underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. What is the most effective measure to prevent a surgical infection in this patient?

opts.t: Transition from IV abx to oral

expl: Hand hygiene is the single most effective infection-prevention measure.

stem: A 35-year-old man came to the emergency department complaining of persistent hiccups. He had undergone sleeve gastrectomy 10 days ago. His vital signs were HR: 112,BP 99/60, 02 Sat 99% on Room Air, Temp: 39C What is the best next step in his management following resuscitation?

opts.t: Reassure patient that hiccups are expected and will go away
Consult pulmonology to manage his hiccups
Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen to rule out leak or abscess
Prescribe chlorpromazine and discharge the patient

expl: Fever, tachycardia and hiccups (diaphragmatic irritation) after sleeve gastrectomy suggest a staple-line leak/subphrenic abscess → CT abdomen.

stem: A 56-year-old gentleman is in the operating room for emergency laparotomy for perforated duodenal ulcer. Earlier he presented with acute abdomen and was hemodynamically unstable. After surgery, what is the most appropriate management of this patient to decrease morbidity from post-operative complications?

opts.t: Gastrograffin upper GI series to rule out leak on post op day 1
CBC every 6 hours to rule out bleeding
CT abdomen in 48 hours to rule out collection

expl: A patient who was haemodynamically unstable before emergency laparotomy needs ICU care to reduce postoperative morbidity.

stem: Patient did a sleeve gastrectomy surgery case, 1 week later developed overt gastric leak. Hemodynamically unstable, peritonitis symptoms and signs. after resuscitation and stabilizing what’s the most appropriate management?

opts.t: percutaneous drainage and control of leak.
surgical control of leak, local irrigation, and appropriate drainage

expl: An overt leak with peritonitis in an unstable patient → after resuscitation, surgical control: washout, drainage ± repair. Stents/percutaneous drainage are for stable patients with contained leaks.

stem: a Lady presented to you 4 weeks after ear piercing with a scar within the ear piercing. what’s the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Source key C. A raised scar confined to the piercing appearing within weeks = hypertrophic scar. Keloids usually appear later and extend beyond the wound.

why.A: Usually appears months later and grows beyond the wound.

stem: A patient complains of a headache 2 days after a lumbar puncture, which of the following is the best initial management:
expl: Post-dural-puncture headache → initial conservative care: analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs, caffeine), hydration, rest. Blood patch is for persistent/severe headache. (The source writes "Answer C".)

why.B: Lying down helps; avoiding it is wrong.

stem: An 18 years old woman developed urticaria and wheezing following IV injection contrast for abdominal CT scan. Her Bp is 120/80 , pulse 120/minute and respiratory rate was 30/min. Which ONE of the following is the appropriate immediate therapy?
srcNote: Source note (436 A Q23): The question was cancelled because more than 50% answered wrong. The course organizer told us the answer is Epinephrine. Source note (429 F Q19): anaphylaxic shock
expl: Urticaria + wheeze after contrast = anaphylaxis → epinephrine (IM). The question was cancelled because many answered wrong; the organizer confirmed epinephrine.

stem: 24-year old female patient, 4 days post exploratory laparotomy after perforated appendix, presented with distended abdomen , discomfort, vomiting and constipation. Blood test showed leukocytosis and vitals were normal. X-ray showed multiple air - fluid level What is the possible diagnosis?
expl: Distension, vomiting and air-fluid levels 4 days after laparotomy for perforated appendix with normal vitals → paralytic ileus.

stem: 50 year old patient post Roux-e-Y procedure after 4 years he came with severe colics in the center of the abdomen he was hemodynamically stable and all his vitals were alright. Which of the following is most commonly the cause of his presentation?
expl: Source key: adhesions (commonest cause of SBO after any abdominal surgery). After Roux-en-Y, internal hernia is the classic special concern for intermittent colicky pain.

why.D: Marginal ulcer causes epigastric pain, not colic.

stem: A patient who had sleeve gastrectomy complicated by a leak. What is the management?

opts.t: Percutaneous drain and correction of leak
Surgical drainage, wash out and correction of leak
Roux en Y surgery as first line management

expl: Source key: surgical drainage, washout and repair of the leak. (Stable patients with contained leaks can be managed with percutaneous drainage/endoscopic stents.)

why.A: An option for small contained leaks.
why.D: Conversion to RYGB is a later salvage option.

stem: A patient post gastric sleeve developed tachycardia and decreased urine output. Which one of the following is the reason?
expl: Tachycardia (often the earliest sign) and falling urine output after sleeve gastrectomy → staple-line leak until proven otherwise.

why.A: Possible, but tachycardia after sleeve = leak classically.

stem: After 24 h of anesthesia and hemorrhoidectomy. a patient came in with a headache. What is the initial management?
srcNote: Pricples & Practice: persistence of headach to more than 12h require a blood patch. more explination: Treatment for spinal headaches begins conservatively. Your doctor may recommend getting bed rest, drinking plenty of fluids, consuming caffeine and taking oral pain relievers.If your headache hasn't improved within 24 hours, your doctor might suggest an epidural blood patch. This is the usual treatment for persistent spinal headaches that don't resolve on their own.
expl: Source key: epidural blood patch (the source note says persistent headache >12–24 h → blood patch). The other versions of this question key bed rest as the INITIAL step.

why.C: Initial step in the other versions.

stem: A young female pt underwent Hemorrhoidectomy under epidural anesthesia, complaining of headache. Which of the following is the initial management?
srcNote: Definitive treatment is epidural blood patch BUT initial treatment is bed rest + fluids + caffeine + oral analgesia.
expl: Post-dural-puncture headache: initial = bed rest, fluids, caffeine and analgesia; definitive = epidural blood patch.

stem: Female patient underwent emergency hysterectomy. 2 days post op the wound drains (clear fluid) 800ml/24h and the urethra 700ml/24h. What is the most likely cause?
expl: 800 mL/day of clear fluid from the drain plus only 700 mL/day of urine after hysterectomy → urine leaking from an injured ureter (one kidney drains into the abdomen).

why.B: Bladder injury would reduce urethral urine more and show haematuria.

stem: Pt underwent gastric sleeve, developed gastric fistula. What abnormality will be found?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: Gastric fluid is rich in HCl and K⁺ → a gastric fistula causes hypokalemia (with hypochloremic alkalosis).

why.D: Urine K⁺ may rise in alkalosis but hypokalemia is keyed.

stem: A 75 year old man underwent right inguinal hernia repair 12 hours ago and he is unable to void since the surgery. On examination, the lower abdomen is distended to the umbilicus. What is the next step of management?
expl: Acute urinary retention after hernia repair with a distended bladder → decompress with a urethral (Foley) catheter.

stem: You just complete an oncologic resection procedure on a patient and plan to start that patient on chemotherapy. How long should you ideally wait before starting the first cycle of chemotherapy to minimize the chances of wound healing problems?
srcNote: (Skin and soft tissue lesions) (From a wound healing perspective the third phase of wound healing is completed by the third week and it is the phase most susceptible to factors that delay wound healing such as chemotherapy, thus starting chemotherapy after 3 weeks ensures wound healing does not get delayed, therefore the answer is B)(Essentials of plastic book had a question with the same scenario and the answer was to wait for 10-14 days to minimize healing problems)
expl: Chemotherapy impairs the proliferative phase of wound healing; starting ~3 weeks after surgery avoids wound problems (other sources say 10–14 days).

stem: a young female pt underwent Haemorrhoidectomy under epidural anesthesia, complaining of headache. Which of the following is the last definitive management?
srcNote: (Practical Procedures and Investigation of Surgical Patients)
expl: The definitive ("last") treatment for persistent post-dural-puncture headache is an epidural blood patch.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presented to the surgery clinic for a large lump in her anterior neck. After examination and investigation, she was found to have multiple nodular lesion on the thyroid gland and was booked for a thyroidectomy. Two weeks later she presents to the ER with lethargy, irritability and numbness in her fingers and toes. Which of the following will likely be positive in this patient?
expl: Numbness of fingers/toes and irritability after thyroidectomy = hypocalcaemia → Chvostek's sign (facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve).

stem: A 70-year-old women presented to the surgery clinic for a large lump in her anterior neck. After examination and investigation, she was found to have multiple nodular lesion on the thyroid gland and was booked for a thyroidectomy. Two weeks later she presents to the ER with lethargy, irritability and numbness in her fingers and toes. Which of the following will likely be positive in this patient?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patients) Source note (432 F Q31): hypocalcaemia as a complication of parathyroid injury post thyroidectomy. Source note (431 A Q14): Chvostek's sign is the twitching of the facial muscles in response to tapping over the area of the facial nerve. Trousseau's sign is carpopedal spasm caused by inflating the blood-pressure cuff to a level above systolic pressure for 3 minutes
expl: Hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy → Chvostek's sign (facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve).

why.C: Kussmaul = JVP rise on inspiration (constrictive pericarditis).

stem: A 32-year-old man underwent open appendectomy for perforated appendicitis. He was started on therapeutic course of intravenous Cefuroxime and metronidazole. Five days later, the wound became painful, swollen, red with pus discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
srcNote: (Surgical Infections) Source note (432 F Q53): drain it
expl: Pus in a wound = an abscess that needs drainage — open the wound. Changing/increasing antibiotics doesn't treat pus.

stem: A 33-year old woman admitted as gallstones for day case laparoscopic cholecystectomy. After surgery the patient was transferred to the ward. Which of the following is needed to be assessed during the post-operative?
srcNote: (Surgical Complications) Source note (433 A Q20): included in immediate postoperative monitoring (davidson summary box 9.1)
expl: After a lap chole the first thing to assess on the ward is cardio-respiratory status (airway, breathing, circulation after anesthesia). Port-site hernia, infection and wound problems appear later.

stem: A 51 years old male underwent exploratory laparotomy 3 weeks ago. Patient presented to the ER with right epigastric pain for 2 weeks. Patient was febrile (38.8) and with high WBCs (18,000) CT abdomen showed large intra-abdominal collection (12*18 cm ) what is the most appropriate next step ?
expl: A large intra-abdominal collection after laparotomy → image-guided percutaneous drainage first (compilers marked "not sure").

why.D: Reserved for failed drainage or peritonitis.

stem: A 32y\o man, 7 days post right hemicolectomy with NGT in situ, found in arterial blood gases to have PH 7.5 and high bicarbonate level. Which of the following is possible associated abnormalities?
srcNote: Source note (429 F Q58): Metabolic alkalosis limits the ability of the kidneys to conserve potassium and predispose to hypokalaemia. Reference: Davidson 6th ed. ch. 1 p. 10, 16.
expl: NG drainage → metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.5, high HCO₃) associated with hypokalemia (and hypochloremia, paradoxical aciduria).

stem: Which of the following is part of SIRs?
expl: SIRS criteria = temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, WBC.

stem: A 47-year-old lady underwent small bowel resection with anastomosis, then she developed high output small bowel fistula ( 700ml/day ) Which of the following is the expected electrolyte/metabolic abnormality?
srcNote: (Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients) Source note (429 F Q59): Intestinal secretions are high in bicarbonate and potassium, Which means, the body is excreting a large amount of both potassium and bicarbonate leading to metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia
expl: High-output small-bowel fistula loses HCO₃-rich fluid → metabolic acidosis.

stem: 68 year old female had hypovolemic shock due to splenic rupture and underwent splenectomy, and was transfused 8 packed RBCs. 3 days post op she started to have fever (38.2) blood culture showed gram negative bacilli what is the most likely cause of her bacteraemia?
srcNote: Source note (432 F Q4): “As described above, the redistribution of cardiac output observed in shock leads to a marked reduction in splanchnic blood flow. In the stomach, the resulting mucosal hypoperfusion and hypoxia predispose to stress ulceration and haemorrhage. In the intestine, movement (translocation) of bacteria and/or bacterial endotoxin from the lumen to the portal vein and then systemic circulation is thought to be a key mechanism underlying the development of SIRS and multiple organ failure” -Davidsons page 22
expl: Shock reduces splanchnic perfusion → gut mucosal ischemia → bacteria/endotoxin translocate into the portal and systemic circulation → gram-negative bacteremia.

why.B: Possible but not the keyed mechanism.

stem: A 12 years old girl had appendectomy for perforated appendicitis. Which of the following is the commonest long-term complication?
expl: The commonest long-term complication after appendectomy (especially perforated) is adhesive small-bowel obstruction. Infertility risk from perforated appendicitis in girls is debated and less common.

stem: 25 y\o man, involved in RTA and underwent exploratory laparotomy. Splenectomy and repair of liver laceration. During surgery he received 12 units of pack red blood cell. Which of the following is the possible side effect of blood transfusion in this patient?
srcNote: ( Miscellaneous ) Source note (430 A Q68): hypothermia, dilutional coagulopathy, hypocalcemia/hypomagnesemia & citrate toxicity, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis Source note (429 F Q20): massive blood transfusion complication. Refer to table: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/780074-overview#a5
expl: Stored blood contains citrate anticoagulant; massive transfusion → citrate toxicity (binds calcium → hypocalcemia).

stem: 65 y\o diabetic male, admitted for laparoscopic trans-abdominal repair of right inguinal hernia under general anesthesia. Which of the following is possible post-operative complication in recovery room?
expl: A diabetic after GA is at risk of silent MI in the recovery room. DIC, wound infection and jaundice are not expected then.

stem: A 15 y/o woman Underwent appendectomy for acute appendicitis. One hour later collapsed in the recovery room. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
srcNote: (Surgical complications) Source note (429 F Q22): due to bleeding.
expl: Collapse within an hour of surgery is most often due to bleeding (hypovolemic shock).

stem: A 55 y\o man, 2nd day post-total gastrectomy with excessive opiate administration found in arterial blood gas to have PH 7.3. He was febrile with normal pulse and blood pressure. Which of the following is the possible associated electrolyte and acid-base abnormality?
srcNote: ( Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients ) resp depression due to opiate use Source note (429 F Q60): Opiate causes depression of the respiratory centre and hence an increase in PaCO2 which cause respiratory acidosis.
expl: Excess opiates → respiratory depression → CO₂ retention → respiratory acidosis (high PaCO₂).

stem: A 45 y/o man who underwent exploratory laparotomy for adhesive small bowel obstruction 3 days back with nasogastric drainage was found to have distended abdomen with constipation. His serum potassium level was 2.5 mmol/l (normal 3.5-5). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Administration of potassium chloride through the Nasogastric tube
Intravenous infusion of dextrose with insulin

srcNote: ( Principles of Fluids and Electrolytes Balance in Surgical Patients ) Source note (430 A Q34): never give potassium bolus can cause heart abnormalities
expl: Severe hypokalemia (2.5) causing ileus → IV KCl infusion at a controlled rate; never as a bolus (cardiac arrest).

stem: A 55 y/o woman underwent abdominal computed tomography for investigation of acute diffuse abdominal pain. During the procedure she devolved difficulty in breathing with pulse rate of 45/min and blood pressure of 90/55 mmHg. Which of the following characterize this condition?
expl: Contrast anaphylaxis → mediator-induced vasodilation and capillary leak → redistribution of intravascular volume (relative hypovolemia).

stem: A 29 y/o man admitted to intensive care unit with massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to duodenal ulcer. While he is receiving blood transfusion, he developed fever, chest tightness and hypotension. His urine was dark in color. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, chest tightness, hypotension and dark urine (hemoglobinuria) during transfusion = acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

why.A: Doesn't explain dark urine during transfusion.

stem: A 32 y/o man victim of motor vehicle accident with massive intra-abdominal bleeding. Received 10 units of packed red blood cells within 12 hours. Which of the following is the most common complication this patient may have?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: Stored blood leaks K⁺ from lysed cells → hyperkalemia after massive transfusion (also citrate toxicity/hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy).

why.B: Acidosis early (alkalosis later from citrate metabolism).

stem: A 46 y/o diabetic man admitted through emergency department with diagnosis of ascending cholangitis. He was started on therapeutic course of intravenous amoxicillin, metronidazole and gentamicin. Three days later the serum urea and creatinine steadily elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
expl: Gentamicin is nephrotoxic; a rising creatinine means stop it (and switch to a non-nephrotoxic agent).

stem: 35 y\o male who is 5 days post appendectomy complained of pain redness and swelling of operation site with some purulent discharge. He has fever. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
expl: Infected wound with pus → remove sutures and drain.

why.B: Not the standard approach for a superficial wound abscess.

stem: A 70 year old female presented to the surgery clinic for a large lump in her neck, examination and investigation she was found to have multiple nodular lesions. She was booked for thyroidectomy. Two weeks after the surgery she presented to the emergency with lethargy, irritability her fingers and toes. Which one of the following will likely be positive in this patient?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient ) (Parathyroid resection causes hypocalcemia)
expl: Lethargy, irritability and numbness of fingers/toes after thyroidectomy → hypocalcemia (parathyroid injury).

stem: 45 y/o woman underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstone. Which is included in the first day post-operative?
srcNote: ( Surgical Complications ) Source note (429 F Q44): “Optimal postoperative care requires clinical assessment and monitoring” Davidson page number 119
expl: Post-op day 1 care relies on clinical assessment and monitoring; routine imaging isn't needed.

stem: While on duty you are called to the recovery room to see a 50 y/o male post appendectomy. Upon your arrival you see him drowsy and unresponsive. His Pulse and blood pressure are normal and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air.What is the most likely cause of his decreased level of consciousness?
expl: Drowsy, unresponsive in recovery with SpO₂ 90% and normal pulse/BP → hypoventilation/respiratory failure from residual anesthetic or opioids.

stem: A 70 y/o male patient, 6 days post-elective surgery, was brought to the emergency department with decreased level of consciousness. On examination he appears flushed and his extremities are (something ... Couldn’t remember) touch. His pulse 120/min, BP: 70/45 and oxygen saturation is 96% on 4L O2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Flushed warm skin, hypotension, tachycardia and altered consciousness after surgery → septic (distributive) shock (compilers "not sure").

why.B: Cardiogenic shock gives cold, clammy extremities.

stem: A 30 y/o man is admitted to surgery department for huge abscess drainage. He was started on antibiotics and analgesics, but complains of sudden severe shortness of breath. There is no chest pain, but he is cyanosed and there was diffuse wheezing over the chest. His BP: 70/30 mmHg and HR is … tachycardic ? couldn’t remember. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: ? Mostly because after the administration of antibiotics he developed these symptoms
expl: Sudden dyspnea, diffuse wheeze, cyanosis and hypotension right after starting antibiotics = anaphylaxis.

stem: A 30 y/o male, who is known to have diabetes and hypertension. One day after surgery started to have chest pain and sweeting. His BP: is 80/50 mmHg and pulse is 110/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Surgical Complications) because of the chest pain
expl: Chest pain, sweating and hypotension in a diabetic/hypertensive patient post-op → MI with cardiogenic shock.

stem: A 24 y/o male patient was admitted the surgery trauma unit with multiple injuries 4 weeks ago. He developed sudden onset of chest pain and shortness of breath. His BP: 85/50 mmHg, pulse 110/min, oxygen saturation is 85% on air room, and there is evidence of DVT in the left lower limb. After fluid bolus was given his BP increased to 90/60 mmHg. A CT lung was done and showed a massive pulmonary embolism. Which one of the following is the treatment of choice?
expl: Source key: LMWH — PE with BP responding to fluids is treated with anticoagulation. (Truly massive PE with persistent shock would need thrombolysis.)

stem: A 17 y/o boy was operated for a perforated appendix and was discharged after 5 days in good condition. He came to emergency room 3 days later complaining of mild fever, pain and discharge at the surgical site. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this complication?

opts.t: Give oral antibiotics, reassurance and send home.

expl: Pain, mild fever and discharge at the wound after appendectomy = superficial SSI → open the wound.

why.B: Not needed for a superficial infection.

stem: 60 y/o man who is known to have diabetic, hypertension, congenital hyperbilirubin and spherocytosis, was admitted for investigation of abdominal mass which was proved to be mesenteric cyst. He was operated on day 9. 4 days later he developed a surgical site infection. Which of the following is significantly increase the risk of wound infection in this patient?
expl: Diabetes impairs neutrophil function and healing → significantly increases SSI risk.

why.D: Mild anemia isn't the key factor.

stem: Dextran transfusion leads to which of the following consequences?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient) Source note (426 F Q33): Effect of Dextran on Platelet Adhesiveness and Aggregation. (dextran 40, dextran 70 and dextran 77.5) causes a decrease in adenosine diphosphate induced aggregation and adhesiveness of human platelets.
expl: Dextran coats platelets and reduces their aggregation (antithrombotic effect) and can cause bleeding.

stem: Which of the following is a complication of obesity surgery?
srcNote: (Upper gastrointestinal and bariatric surgery, abdominal wall, umbilicus, herniae, and retroperitoneum), This is because as the body metabolises fat during rapid Weight Loss, it causes the liver to secrete extra cholesterol into the bile, potentially causing gallstones.
expl: Rapid weight loss after bariatric surgery raises biliary cholesterol → gallstones. Diabetes, hypertension and hypothyroidism improve or aren't caused.

stem: Which ONE of the following is the main difference between Keloids and hypertrophic scars?

opts.t: Keloids extend beyond the original zone of injury

expl: Keloids extend beyond the original wound margins; hypertrophic scars stay within them.

stem: Which of the following is the most serious immediate complication of total thyroidectomy in a patient with Graves' disease?
expl: A neck hematoma can obstruct the airway within hours — the most serious immediate complication (Graves' glands are vascular).

why.D: Common but not the most serious.

stem: A 70 year old diabetic man who is bed ridden for the last 10 years, was brought to the emergency with history of sacral ulcer, which is 15 cm by 15 cm and 2 cm depth. On examination you can see pus discharge and necrotic muscles. How would you expect the wound healing phases to be affected?

opts.t: Decrease in the inflammatory and increase in the proliferative phase.
Increase in the inflammatory and decrease in the proliferative phase.
Increase in the inflammatory and proliferative phase.

expl: A large infected necrotic wound prolongs inflammation (bacteria, necrotic tissue) and, being a large defect healing by secondary intention, needs a long proliferative phase. Diabetes and immobility add to the delay.

stem: All can occur after total thyroidectomy, except:
expl: Thyroidectomy can cause hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia; hypercalcemia is not a complication.

stem: few hours post thyroidectomy female presented with progressive swelling under the incision site, stride, cyanosis:
expl: Expanding neck swelling with stridor and cyanosis after thyroidectomy = hematoma → immediate wound exploration/evacuation.

stem: the most common investigation used in acute venous thrombosis is:
expl: Duplex ultrasound is the standard investigation for DVT.

why.C: Used to rule out in low probability, not to diagnose.

stem: Central line complication (they probably mean which one of the following is not a complication of central line)
expl: Central line complications: pneumothorax, arterial puncture/hematoma, arrhythmia (guidewire), air embolism, infection, thrombosis. Convulsion is not one.

stem: Aorto-enteric fistula all true except

opts.t: Always after surgery of abdominal aortic aneurysm

srcNote: , an aorto-enteric fistula is a connection between the aorta and the intestines, stomach, or esophagus. There can be significant blood loss into the intestines resulting in bloody stool and death. It is usually secondary to an abdominal aortic aneurysm repair.
expl: Aorto-enteric fistula is usually secondary (after AAA graft repair) but primary fistulas from an untreated aneurysm also occur — so "always after AAA surgery" is false. It presents with a herald GI bleed.

stem: young female post appendectomy. She collapsed in the recovery room. All are possible causes EXCEPT:
expl: Early collapse after appendectomy: bleeding, aspiration of vomit, PE (rare) — a wound abscess takes days and doesn't cause collapse in recovery.

stem: blood transfusion can transmit which of the following infection:
expl: Hepatitis B (and C, HIV) is transmitted by blood. Hepatitis A is fecal–oral; hepatitis D needs HBV.

why.C: Needs co-infection with B; B is the classic answer.

stem: complication of Massive transfusion:
expl: Massive transfusion → citrate toxicity (hypocalcemia), hypothermia, hyperkalemia, coagulopathy.

stem: A 37 y/o underwent appendectomy 3 days later developed redness & pus discharge form the wound, the wound re-opened irrigation, debridement and proper dressing was done, which of the following change in this wound healing process with this management?
expl: A reopened, irrigated infected wound heals by secondary intention → longer proliferative phase (granulation, contraction).

stem: A 37 year old underwent laparotomy for perforated appendix 3 days later he developed sever abdominal pain, constipation & vomiting on examination: sluggish bowel sounds, what is the cause for its presentation?
expl: Pain, vomiting, constipation and sluggish bowel sounds 3 days after laparotomy for perforated appendix = paralytic ileus.

why.B: Adhesive obstruction gives hyperactive sounds and comes later.
